claim: Xenopus tadpoles are able to undergo scarless healing and full regeneration of the limb, spinal cord, or tail after injury.
source: In contrast to mammals, Xenopus tadpoles are able to undergo scarless healing and full regeneration of the limb, spinal cord, or tail after injury (Beck et al., 2009; Kakebeen and Wills, 2019; Lee-Liu et al., 2017; Tseng and Levin, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The regenerative capacity of Xenopus declines during metamorphosis and is lost in the adult.
source: While lifelong regenerative healing is a characteristic shared by many amphibians and fish, the regenerative capacity of Xenopus declines during metamorphosis, and is lost in the adult (Filoni and Bosco, 1981; Mitogawa et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Developmental signaling pathways such as Wnt, FGF, BMP, TGF-ß, Notch and Shh are upregulated during regeneration and are required for full regeneration of the limb, tail, and spinal cord.
source: In particular, developmental signaling pathways such as Wnt, FGF, BMP, TGF-ß, Notch and Shh are upregulated, and are required for full regeneration of the limb, tail, and spinal cord (Beck et al., 2003; Ho and Whitman, 2008; Slack et al., 2008; Taniguchi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Numerous genes associated with embryonic development are re-expressed during regeneration.
source: Genome-wide transcriptomic studies have confirmed that numerous genes associated with embryonic development are re-expressed during regeneration (Chang et al., 2017; Lee-Liu et al., 2014; Love et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The regenerating axolotl limb shows a transcriptional convergence between all connective tissue cell types, associated with the formation of the undifferentiated limb blastema.
source: The regenerating axolotl limb shows a transcriptional convergence between all connective tissue cell types, associated with the formation of the undifferentiated limb blastema (Gerber et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In the Xenopus tail, cell type identities are kept clearly intact as regeneration progresses.
source: while in the Xenopus tail, cell type identities are kept clearly intact as regeneration progresses (Aztekin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Pax6 is a highly conserved paired box transcription factor essential for central nervous system development.
source: Pax6 is a highly conserved paired box transcription factor essential for central nervous system development (Bel-Vialar et al., 2007; Osumi et al., 2008; Walther and Gruss, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: GFP expression in transgenic tadpoles includes much of the same domain as the NSC marker Sox2.
source: GFP expression in transgenic tadpoles included much of the same domain as the NSC marker Sox2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D showing colocalization of GFP and Sox2.

claim: Both nuclear Sox2 and cytoplasmic GFP driven by pax6 are localized medially around the central canal, while markers associated with differentiated neurons such as Dcx and neurofilament are largely found in the spinal cord periphery.
source: Notably, both nuclear Sox2 and cytoplasmic GFP driven by pax6 are localized medially around the central canal, while markers associated with differentiated neurons such as Dcx and neurofilament are largely found in the spinal cord periphery (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 1E and 1F showing spatial distribution of markers.

claim: pax6:GFP+ cells can be clearly identified in the regenerating tail as early as 6hpa.
source: We found that pax6:GFP+ cells can be clearly identified in the regenerating tail as early as 6hpa (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1G showing GFP+ cells at 6hpa.

claim: By 24hpa, the GFP+ cells are found in the bulb of the neural ampulla.
source: By 24hpa, the GFP+ cells are found in the bulb of the neural ampulla (Beck et al., 2009; Stefanelli, 1951).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: By 72hpa, GFP+ cells are present all along the anteroposterior axis of the regenerated spinal cord.
source: By 72hpa, GFP+ cells are present all along the anteroposterior axis of the regenerated spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the regeneration timecourse experiment.

claim: The pax6 libraries cluster away from the clustered all-tissue libraries in multi-dimensional scaling analysis.
source: We found that the pax6 libraries cluster away from the clustered all-tissue libraries (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2B showing MDS plot.

claim: The majority of peaks called were located within 500 bp of a transcription start site for both all tissue and pax6 libraries.
source: The majority of peaks called were located within 500 bp of a transcription start site for both all tissue and pax6 libraries, confirming that the majority of ATAC-Seq signal is concentrated in nucleosome-depleted promoters, as expected (Buenrostro et al., 2013; Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2C and citation to the ATAC-Seq method paper.

claim: Upstream of the pax6 TSS, all pax6 library timepoints share a peak that is absent in all-tissue libraries.
source: By contrast, upstream of the pax6 TSS, all pax6 library timepoints share a peak that is absent in all-tissue libraries (Figure 2D, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2D showing IGV browser tracks.

claim: 3604 regions were more accessible in the pax6 libraries than the all-tissue libraries.
source: We identified 3604 regions that were more accessible in the pax6 libraries than the all-tissue libraries, which we assigned to the nearest TSS, and used the associated gene names as input for gene ontology (GO) analysis using gProfileR2 (Raudvere et al., 2019; Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the differential accessibility analysis and reference to Figure 2E-F.

claim: Genes with increased accessibility in pax6:GFP+ cells showed statistically significant enrichment for neural-associated terms such as 'Neurogenesis', 'Nervous system development', and 'Neuron differentiation.'
source: Genes with increased accessibility in pax6:GFP+ cells showed statistically significant enrichment for neural-associated terms such as 'Neurogenesis', 'Nervous system development', and 'Neuron differentiation,' confirming the neural progenitor identity of our pax6:GFP cells (Figure 2F, top, and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 2F.

claim: 5251 regions are more accessible in all-tissue libraries than pax6 libraries.
source: The reverse analysis identified 5251 regions that are more accessible in all-tissue libraries than pax6 libraries, which are associated with broad GO categories relating to ubiquitous cellular processes (i.e. 'Cellular biosynthetic process', 'Transcription from RNA Polymerase II', and Cellular metabolic process') (Figure 2F, bottom, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by the differential accessibility analysis and reference to Figure 2F.

claim: Genes preferentially accessible at 6hpa called six families of GO terms including 'Nephron Tubule Morphogenesis'.
source: We first examined genes associated with regulatory regions that are uniquely accessible at 6hpa. Genes preferentially accessible at 6hpa called six families of GO terms (Figure 3D). Notably, 'Nephron Tubule Morphogenesis' was well represented
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Regions most accessible at the 24hpa timepoint recovered two main families of GO terms, the largest of which was 'Neuron Development'.
source: We then identified regions that were most accessible at the 24hpa timepoint. This analysis recovered two main families of GO terms, the largest of which was 'Neuron Development' (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The majority of genes that call the 'Neuron Development' GO term become more accessible from 6 to 24hpa, but lose that accessibility at 72hpa.
source: Strikingly, the majority of genes that call this GO term become more accessible from 6 to 24hpa, but lose that accessibility at 72hpa (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3H showing heatmap of accessibility.

claim: Processes prioritized at 72hpa resulted in five main GO families being called including 'neuronal precursor cell proliferation'.
source: Finally, we assessed the processes being prioritized at 72hpa. This analysis resulted in five main GO families being called (Figure 3F), including 'neuronal precursor cell proliferation'.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Cell cycle and proliferation related terms were absent at the 6hpa and 24hpa timepoints.
source: Notably, cell cycle and proliferation related terms were absent at the 6hpa and 24hpa timepoints.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of these terms in GO analysis at earlier timepoints.

claim: The regions calling 'neuronal precursor cell proliferation' were all more accessible at 72hpa than the 24hpa timepoint.
source: The regions calling this term were all more accessible at 72hpa than the 24hpa timepoint, however about half were not differentially accessible with respect to the uninjured tail (Figure 3I)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3I showing heatmap of accessibility.

claim: A total of 781 uninjured cells and 296 cells from 24hpa cells fell into neural clusters.
source: A total of 781 uninjured cells and 296 cells from 24hpa cells fell into neural clusters, which comprised NPC/NSCs (defined by expression of sox2), transitioning neurons (neurog1; neurod1), and differentiated neurons (elavl4) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Eight unique sub-clusters were identified within neural cells, including spinal cord progenitors, floor plate progenitors, differentiating neurons, interneurons, motor neurons, vulnerable motor neurons, motor neurons (leptin+), and dopaminergic neurons.
source: To gain the highest-possible resolution of cell types within these broad neural clusters, we subsetted neural cells, re-performed dimensionality reduction and called eight unique sub-clusters, including spinal cord progenitors, floor plate progenitors, differentiating neurons, interneurons, motor neurons, vulnerable motor neurons, motor neurons (leptin+), and dopaminergic neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Unlike the connective tissues in the axolotl limb, which lose cell heterogeneity of gene expression after injury, neural cells in the 24hpa Xenopus spinal cord maintain heterogeneous gene expression.
source: Unlike the connective tissues in the axolotl limb, which lose cell heterogeneity of gene expression after injury (Gerber et al., 2018), neural cells in the 24hpa Xenopus spinal cord maintain heterogeneous gene expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published research on axolotl limb regeneration.

claim: At 24hpa, there is a decrease in the percent of NPCs and differentiating neurons with respect to the uninjured cells.
source: Indeed, at 24hpa, we observe a decrease in the percent of NPCs and differentiating neurons with respect to the uninjured cells (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 4D-G showing sunburst diagrams.

claim: At 24hpa, there is an expansion in differentiated neuronal clusters including interneurons, vulnerable motor neurons, and motor neurons (leptin+).
source: In agreement with our GO analysis of 24hpa ATAC-Seq data, we see an expansion in differentiated neuronal clusters including interneurons, vulnerable motor neurons, and motor neurons (leptin+) at 24hpa.
evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: NSCs are reduced from 38% to 25% at 24hpa.
source: Overall, NSCs are reduced from 38% to 25%, differentiating neurons are reduced from 20% to 10%, and differentiated neurons increase from 42% to 65%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell type proportions in the single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claim: Differentiating neurons are reduced from 20% to 10% at 24hpa.
source: Overall, NSCs are reduced from 38% to 25%, differentiating neurons are reduced from 20% to 10%, and differentiated neurons increase from 42% to 65%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell type proportions in the single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claim: Differentiated neurons increase from 42% to 65% at 24hpa.
source: Overall, NSCs are reduced from 38% to 25%, differentiating neurons are reduced from 20% to 10%, and differentiated neurons increase from 42% to 65%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell type proportions in the single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claim: Motor neurons (leptin+) are virtually absent in the uninjured tail but are abundant at 24hpa.
source: As previously described, we noted that motor neurons (leptin+) are virtually absent in the uninjured tail but are abundant at 24hpa (Aztekin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq data and citation to published research.

claim: The uninjured tail neural lineage has 30% cells predicted in S phase, 16% cells predicted in G2M phase, and 54% cells predicted in G1 phase.
source: The uninjured tail neural lineage has 30% cells predicted in S phase, 16% cells predicted in G2M phase, and 54% cells predicted in G1 phase (Figure 5H/J).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle prediction analysis and reference to Figures 5H/J.

claim: At the 24hpa timepoint, the S phase falls to 17%, G2M falls to 7% and G1 increases to 76%.
source: This distribution shifts markedly at the 24hpa timepoint, where the S phase falls to 17%, G2M falls to 7% and G1 increases to 76% (Figure 4I/K).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle prediction analysis and reference to Figures 4I/K.

claim: l1cam, uchl1, nsg1 and ass1 are strongly expressed in one or more differentiated neuronal populations but are lowly expressed or absent in NPCs and non-neural cell types by scRNA-SEQ.
source: All these genes are strongly expressed in one or more differentiated neuronal populations but are lowly expressed or absent in NPCs and non-neural cell types by scRNA-SEQ (Figure 5A–C,G–I,M–O,S–U).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 5A-C, G-I, M-O, S-U showing gene expression.

claim: l1cam, uchl1, nsg1 and ass1 are most strongly and distinctly expressed in the neural ampulla at 24hpa when examined by ISH.
source: When examined by ISH all four genes are most strongly and distinctly expressed in the neural ampulla at 24hpa (Figure 5E,K,Q,W).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 5E, K, Q, W.

claim: Proliferative cells are significantly more abundant at 72hpa relative to 24hpa.
source: As a further test of the hypothesis that proliferation is not prioritized until 72hpa, we used phospho-histone H3 (PH3) staining to quantify mitotic cells in optical longitudinal sections of the spinal cord that overlap with the pax6 domain, finding that proliferative cells are significantly more abundant at 72hpa relative to 24hpa (Figure 5Y-AA).
evidence: The claim is supported by PH3 staining quantification shown in Figures 5Y-AA.

claim: Meis1 is predicted as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near runx2 and etv1 at 24hpa.
source: One circuit predicts Meis1 as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near runx2 and etv1 at 24hpa, and Etv1 as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near pbx3 at 24hpa (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene regulatory network prediction analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Etv1 is predicted as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near pbx3 at 24hpa.
source: One circuit predicts Meis1 as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near runx2 and etv1 at 24hpa, and Etv1 as a regulatory factor that binds motifs near pbx3 at 24hpa (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene regulatory network prediction analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: etv1, meis1, pbx3, and runx2 are all expressed in the neural cells.
source: In our scRNA-Seq dataset, etv1, meis1, pbx3, and runx2 are all expressed in the neural cells and are therefore reasonable candidates to regulate neural cell fate transitions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claim: pbx3 was the most restricted to the neural lineage among etv1, meis1, pbx3, and runx2.
source: Of these, pbx3 was the most restricted to the neural lineage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,G), and was found in several neuronal cell types.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,G showing gene expression.

claim: Pbx3 and Meis1 are homeodomain transcription factors thought to coregulate targets in B-cell leukemia and proximal-distal patterning of the regenerating axolotl limb.
source: Pbx3 and Meis1 are homeodomain transcription factors thought to coregulate targets in B-cell leukemia and proximal-distal patterning of the regenerating axolotl limb (Li et al., 2016; Mercader et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Meis1 is well-studied for its roles in neural crest and posterior neural fate specification, working together with Pbx1 in Xenopus.
source: In Xenopus, Meis1 is well-studied for its roles in neural crest and posterior neural fate specification, working together with Pbx1 (Kelly et al., 2006; Maeda et al., 2001; Maeda et al., 2002; Salzberg et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Neither pbx3 nor meis1 have been described in neural regeneration.
source: Neither pbx3 nor meis1 have been described in neural regeneration, and so we decided to probe the function of these genes in neural development and regeneration in Xenopus.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of prior literature on these genes in neural regeneration.

claim: A large fraction (26/61) of Pbx3 targets are shared with Meis1.
source: A large fraction (26/61) of Pbx3 targets are shared with Meis1 (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6B showing Venn diagram of target regions.

claim: Meis1's target peaks are preferentially increased in accessibility at 24hpa.
source: Meis1's target peaks are preferentially increased in accessibility at 24hpa, while Pbx3's are overall increased at 72hpa.
evidence: The claim is supported by the ATAC-Seq differential accessibility analysis.

claim: Pbx3's target peaks are overall increased at 72hpa.
source: Meis1's target peaks are preferentially increased in accessibility at 24hpa, while Pbx3's are overall increased at 72hpa.
evidence: The claim is supported by the ATAC-Seq differential accessibility analysis.

claim: Following injury, at 24hpa, expression of meis1 increased to 30% of all neural cells.
source: Following injury, at 24hpa, expression of meis1 increased to 30% of all neural cells (Figure 6F, upper right), driven by increases in interneurons (IN), dopaminergic neuron (DN), and especially motor neuron (MN) clusters (Figure 6E, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 6E and 6F showing gene expression.

claim: At 24hpa expression of pbx3 increased to 11% of all neural cells.
source: At 24hpa expression of pbx3 increased to 11% of all neural cells (Figure 6F bottom right), driven by a strong increase in motor neuron expression (Figure 6E, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 6E and 6F showing gene expression.

claim: At stage 41, both meis1 and pbx3 are expressed in the uninjured brain and spinal cord.
source: At stage 41, both meis1 and pbx3 are expressed in the uninjured brain and spinal cord (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 6G-J.

claim: By 24hpa, expression of both meis1 and pbx3 increases in the spinal cord.
source: However, by 24hpa, expression of both factors increases in the spinal cord (Figure 6M,N).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 6M,N.

claim: By 72hpa, expression of meis1 and pbx3 persists more weakly in the spinal cord.
source: By 72hpa, expression persists more weakly in the spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization observations.

claim: Knockdown of either Meis1 or Pbx3 resulted in a similar phenotype in stage 41 tadpoles that included small or missing eyes, a shorter anteroposterior body axis and reduced pigment cell population.
source: Knockdown of either Meis1 or Pbx3 resulted in a similar phenotype in stage 41 tadpoles that included small or missing eyes, a shorter anteroposterior body axis and reduced pigment cell population (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The second set of morpholinos phenocopy the original morpholino injections.
source: We followed up on these phenotypes by repeating the injections with a second set of morpholinos against Pbx3 and Meis1. The second set of morpholinos phenocopy the original morpholino injections (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: CRISPR guide RNAs targeting meis1 or pbx3 together with Cas9 protein phenocopy the morpholino effects.
source: As a further confirmation, we designed and injected CRISPR guide RNAs targeting each of these genes together with Cas9 protein at the 4 cell stage, and were able to phenocopy the morpholino effects with this strategy as well (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G-J.

claim: Stage 41 morphants stained with anti-neurofilament antibody had mispatterned spinal cord and intersomitic axons.
source: When we stained stage 41 morphants with anti-neurofilament antibody, we found that their spinal cord and intersomitic axons were mispatterned, suggesting Meis1 and Pbx3 are necessary for proper development of the nervous system (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B-F.

claim: Neither Meis1 nor Pbx3 vivo-MO caused gross morphological defects when delivered at late tailbud stage.
source: Neither vivo-MO caused gross morphological defects when delivered this way, but both vivo-MOs resulted in reduced axons in the spinal cord as assayed by neurofilament stains at stage 41 (Figure 7C,D), relative to control tadpoles injected with tracer only (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by vivo-morpholino experiments shown in Figures 7B-D.

claim: Both Meis1 and Pbx3 vivo-MOs resulted in reduced axons in the spinal cord as assayed by neurofilament stains at stage 41.
source: Neither vivo-MO caused gross morphological defects when delivered this way, but both vivo-MOs resulted in reduced axons in the spinal cord as assayed by neurofilament stains at stage 41 (Figure 7C,D), relative to control tadpoles injected with tracer only (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by vivo-morpholino experiments shown in Figures 7B-D.

claim: At 72hpa, both Pbx3 and Meis1 knockdown tadpoles have reduced and disorganized neurofilament staining relative to tracer-injected controls.
source: At 72hpa, both Pbx3 and Meis1 knockdown tadpoles have reduced and disorganized neurofilament staining relative to tracer-injected controls (Figure 7F,G, compare with E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7E-G.

claim: Both Meis1 and Pbx3 knockdown tadpoles have significantly shorter regenerated tails and spinal cords relative to tracer-injected control tadpoles at 72hpa.
source: We quantified the length of the regenerated tail in control and knockdown tadpoles at 72hpa, and found that both Meis1 and Pbx3 knockdown tadpoles have significantly shorter regenerated tails and spinal cords relative to tracer-injected control tadpoles (Figure 7K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Spinal cord area is significantly reduced in both Meis1 and Pbx3 morphants at 72hpa.
source: Spinal cord area (measured in confocal optical longitudinal sections) is also significantly reduced in both morphants at 72hpa (Figure 7L)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 7L.

claim: The density of PH3 positive nuclei is not significantly changed relative to controls in Meis1 and Pbx3 morphants.
source: although the density of PH3 positive nuclei is not significantly changed relative to controls (Figure 7H–J,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figures 7H-J,M.

claim: Meis1 and Pbx3 are required for proper neural development and for proper regeneration of the tail and spinal cord.
source: We conclude that Meis1 and Pbx3 are not only required for proper neural development but also for proper regeneration of the tail and spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined results of morpholino and CRISPR experiments.

claim: By isolating neural progenitors, we are able to identify a unique chromatin landscape for these cells, including regulatory peaks that cannot be detected in bulk tissue analysis.
source: By isolating neural progenitors, we are able to identify a unique chromatin landscape for these cells, including regulatory peaks that cannot be detected in bulk tissue analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on the ATAC-Seq analysis comparing pax6+ cells to bulk tissue.

claim: pax6+ neural progenitors place a high priority on neuronal differentiation, and specifically on formation of interneurons and motor neuron subtypes by 24hpa.
source: We find that pax6+ neural progenitors place an early priority on neuronal differentiation, and specifically on formation of interneurons and motor neuron subtypes by 24hpa, shown as a model in Figure 8A–C.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined ATAC-Seq and scRNA-Seq analysis.

claim: By 24hpa, pax6+ neural progenitors accessibilize genes associated with proliferation and self-renewal at 72hpa.
source: Using both ATAC-Seq and scRNA-Seq, we show that by 24 hr post amputation (hpa), pax6+ neural progenitors place a high priority on differentiation to motor and interneuron subtypes, and only later at 72hpa do they accessibilize genes associated with proliferation and self-renewal.
evidence: The claim is supported by the ATAC-Seq analysis showing differential accessibility at 72hpa.

claim: pax6+ progenitors prioritize differentiation before proliferation in regeneration, which represents an intriguing counterpoint to embryonic development.
source: Our finding that pax6+ progenitors prioritize differentiation before proliferation in regeneration represents an intriguing counterpoint to embryonic development, in which regional-specific proliferative neural progenitors can only later make the decision to undergo neurogenesis and exit the cell cycle (Hardwick et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to published research on embryonic development.

claim: There is little proliferation after tail amputation prior to 48hpa.
source: Our model agrees with numerous findings that there is little proliferation after tail amputation prior to 48hpa (Contreras et al., 2009; Gaete et al., 2012; Love et al., 2011; Pelzer et al., 2020; Tsujioka et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Bulk RNA-Seq analysis shows a transcriptional upregulation of axonogenesis and other neuronal differentiation genes during regeneration.
source: and with bulk RNA-Seq analysis showing a transcriptional upregulation of axonogenesis and other neuronal differentiation genes (Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The identities of specific neural cell types are readily assigned to the same clusters both before and after tail transection in Xenopus.
source: The identities of specific neural cell types are readily assigned to the same clusters both before and after tail transection in Xenopus.
evidence: The claim is based on the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: In the axolotl limb, scRNA-Seq shows that different connective tissue cell types lose their unique transcriptional identities early in regeneration and converge on a similar signature, as the blastema forms.
source: In the axolotl limb, scRNA-Seq shows that different connective tissue cell types lose their unique transcriptional identities early in regeneration and converge on a similar signature, as the blastema forms (Gerber et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Diverse cell types retain well-discriminated transcriptional signatures as regeneration proceeds in Xenopus.
source: While the early Xenopus tail regenerate has also been described as a blastema (Gargioli and Slack, 2004; Tsujioka et al., 2015), its parallels to the axolotl blastema have been debated (Mochii et al., 2007), and our study confirms that diverse cell types retain well-discriminated transcriptional signatures as regeneration proceeds.
evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Pbx3 and Meis1 are expressed in the regenerating spinal cord, with increased expression in motor neuron subtypes during regeneration.
source: We show that these factors are both expressed in the regenerating spinal cord, with increased expression in motor neuron subtypes during regeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and scRNA-Seq data.

claim: Loss of function of either Pbx3 or Meis1 results in disorganized neurofilament outgrowth with a failure of successful axial tissue regeneration.
source: Loss of function of either factor results in disorganized neurofilament outgrowth with a failure of successful axial tissue regeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino and CRISPR experiments.

claim: Pbx3 and Meis1 are predicted to bind upstream of several dozen differentially accessible neuronal differentiation factors.
source: These factors are predicted to bind upstream of several dozen differentially accessible neuronal differentiation factors and are thus well-placed to drive the prioritization of neuronal differentiation we observe.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis of ATAC-Seq data.

claim: Loss of either Pbx3 or Meis1 does not result in a failure to form neurofilaments, but does result in grossly disrupted organization of neurofilaments and reduced regeneration of the tail and spinal cord.
source: Loss of either factor does not result in a failure to form neurofilaments, but does result in grossly disrupted organization of neurofilaments and reduced regeneration of the tail and spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino and CRISPR experiments.

claim: Pbx3 and Meis1 may contribute to the ongoing differentiation of neuronal structures from 24hpa to 72hpa.
source: We therefore propose that Pbx3 and Meis1 contribute to the ongoing differentiation of neuronal structures from 24hpa to 72hpa (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is based on the combined ATAC-Seq and scRNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Loss of either Pbx3 or Meis1 results in reduced tail regeneration overall, which may be due to interactions between regenerating nerves or neuronal structures and other axial structures.
source: Intriguingly, loss of either Pbx3 or Meis1 results in reduced tail regeneration overall. This may be due to interactions between regenerating nerves or neuronal structures and other axial structures, as regeneration of appendages has been shown to be nerve dependent in Xenopus and other systems (Farkas and Monaghan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on morpholino experiments and citation to published research.

claim: Pbx3 and Meis1 are known to heterodimerize and coregulate targets upstream of hoxa9 during leukemia progression.
source: Pbx3 and Meis1 are known to heterodimerize and coregulate targets upstream of hoxa9 during leukemia progression (Li et al., 2016; Machon et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Meis1 partners with the related protein Pbx1 in axolotl limb regeneration and neural development.
source: Meis1 also partners with the related protein Pbx1 in axolotl limb regeneration and neural development (French et al., 2007; Mercader et al., 2005; Mojsin and Stevanovic, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Neither pbx3 nor meis1 have been studied in neural regeneration.
source: Neither pbx3 nor meis1 have been studied in neural regeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of prior literature on these genes in neural regeneration.

claim: Neural progenitors temporally uncouple their regulation of differentiation and proliferation, placing an earlier priority on differentiation of motor neuron subtypes.
source: We show that neural progenitors temporally uncouple their regulation of differentiation and proliferation, placing an earlier priority on differentiation of motor neuron subtypes.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined ATAC-Seq and scRNA-Seq analysis.

claim: The temporal uncoupling of differentiation and proliferation in neural progenitors represents an intriguing contrast to embryonic development.
source: This new model represents an intriguing contrast to embryonic development.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to embryonic development.

claim: pbx3 and meis1 are critical regulators of neural development and regeneration.
source: We computationally identify multiple candidate regulators of neural progenitor fate decisions in a regenerative context, and specifically highlight pbx3 and meis1 as critical regulators of neural development and regeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined computational analysis and loss-of-function experiments.
